chapter.title: Introduction
chapter.para: ooRexx/Python connects two interpreters that run in the same process: an ooRexx interpreter and a CPython interpreter. Each side sees the other's objects as its own, by reference: nothing is copied but the simplest values (strings and numbers), and a message sent to a proxy reaches the object on the other side.

listitem.para: ooRexx using Python. A Rexx program that requires python.cls gets the environment object &py;, Python's builtins plus a few helpers. Any Python object is a instance, used with ordinary Rexx messages.
Python using ooRexx. A Python program that imports the module oorexx creates interpreter instances (), runs Rexx programs, routines and expressions, and uses any Rexx object as an .

Both at once. The two directions nest freely, on any thread: Rexx calls Python, which calls back a Rexx object, which calls Python again. A Rexx class can extend a Python class, so that Python calls Rexx methods where it would call its own (see ).

example.title: ooRexx using Python
example.programlisting:
np = .py~import("numpy") m = np~array(((1, 2), (3, 4))) say m~sum m~shape -- the sum and the shape say .py~round(np~linalg~det(m), 2) -- the determinant
::requires "python.cls"

example.title: Python using ooRexx
example.programlisting:
import oorexx
with oorexx.Interpreter() as rexx: print(rexx.eval("6 * 7")) times = rexx.routine("use arg a, b; return a * b") print(times(6, 7)) d = rexx.eval(".directory~new") # a Rexx object d["NAME"] = "Ann" print(len(d), d["NAME"])

section.title: Requirements
section.para: Python 3.9 or later. The bridge uses only Python's Stable ABI (PEP 384), so the same binary works with CPython 3.9 and every later version, with no virtual environments and no per-version builds.

ooRexx 5.3.0 r13278 or later. The bridge uses only ooRexx's public native API: the interpreter needs no change, and the bridge is an extension package, like rxsock or BSF4ooRexx. It needs ooRexx's logicalwrapper.cls, new in r13278 ().
The bridge runs on Linux, macOS and Windows.

section.title: The Parts of the Bridge

listitem.para: The Rexx side: the classes and routines described in this book. A Rexx program uses the bridge with ::requires "python.cls".
The bridge itself: at the same time the Python module oorexx and the native code of python.cls.

varlistentry.term: librexxpython.so (librexxpython.dylib on macOS, rexxpython.dll on Windows)

listitem.para: The ooRexx package that python.cls requires. When a program started by rexx needs Python, it finds a Python, loads it, and hands over to the bridge.

section.para: The installer of the binary release (rexx install) puts them into the ooRexx installation and makes the module importable from the Python it is given (on Windows, the release's installer program does the same with a wizard); the release's README.md explains it, and how to use the bridge without installing it.

section.title: Which Python
section.para: A program started by Python uses that Python. A program started by rexx uses the Python named by the environment variable ORX_PYTHON (a full path to its executable), or else the one the installer recorded (a line python = executable in the file oorexxpython.cfg, next to the bridge), or else the python3 on the PATH (python on Windows). It sees that Python's installed packages, a virtual environment's too.
The Python is loaded once per process, the first time a program requires python.cls, and stays until the process ends: every interpreter instance of the process shares it.

section.title: The Names in this Book
section.para: Rexx's names are those of python.cls: the environment object &py; (an instance of the class ), the classes PyObject, PyArrayProxy, PyKwArgs, PyOutputStream and PyInputStream, and the routines py.import, py.box, py.kw, py.extend and py.redirectTo. Python's names are those of the module oorexx: Interpreter, RexxObject, RexxError and CommandContext.
The examples' outputs come from CPython; a value printed by Python (a list, a float) is printed as Python prints it.
